description: Catalyst CR is more than a team—we are curious minds brought together by science, technology, and the excitement of creating something meaningful.  We combine engineering, AI, automation, electronics, and creativity, but our greatest strength is how we learn, collaborate, and build together. We believe great ideas happen when different minds connect.
summary:
We developed AstroVital AI, a research prototype that pairs an experimental chest-worn device with an offline-first dashboard designed to monitor up to four astronauts. It brings together vital signs, ECG signals when supported by the hardware, and crew health check-ins. The dashboard shows trends, explains what each indicator means, and flags missing or unreliable readings.

On long-duration missions, limited communication with Earth can delay guidance when a crew member’s health changes. AstroVital AI gives crews a shared view of their health data, even without internet access, so they can spot changes, document observations, and decide when a concern needs follow-up.

To protect sensitive crew health data, we are developing encryption for data transmitted from the ESP32 device to the application’s FastAPI backend. Our security design also includes multifactor authentication (MFA) for access to the dashboard.
details:
We created a Google Drive folder with materials showing the AstroVital AI hardware and software prototypes, how they work, and how they work together.

The folder also includes the software MVP (Minimum Viable Product) and a user manual available in English and Spanish. The manual walks you through the application step by step, showing each screen and explaining how to navigate the dashboard and use its features.

To review the project, open the Google Drive folder, choose the manual in your preferred language, and follow the walkthrough as you explore the software MVP and the hardware demonstration materials.

  1. What does your project do, and how does it work?

AstroVital AI is a research prototype designed to support collaborative and autonomous crew health monitoring during long-duration space missions. An experimental chest-worn device uses an ESP32 to collect readings from several sensors and transmit them to a FastAPI backend.

A shared dashboard is designed to monitor up to four astronauts, centralizing vital signs, ECG signals when supported by the hardware, and self-reported health check-ins. The platform integrates physiological measurements, physical activity indicators, perceived fatigue, and longitudinal health trends when sufficient data is available.

When an alert appears, the crew can see who it concerns, which signal triggered it, and how the reading has changed over time. The dashboard also flags missing or unreliable readings. Its offline-first design aims to keep core monitoring available over a local network when internet access is unavailable.

Additionally, the platform includes an informational module based on the five human spaceflight hazards identified by NASA’s Human Research Program: radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and closed environments. This module connects these challenges with the prototype’s current capabilities and future development opportunities.

  1. What are its benefits and intended impact?

A shared view helps the crew notice changes, review alerts, and document observations. By combining physiological measurements with self-reported information, AstroVital AI provides additional context for understanding changes in an astronaut’s well-being.

If an astronaut reports feeling unwell, the crew can review recent readings and check-ins together to decide when a concern needs follow-up.

Our goal is to give crews more autonomy when guidance from Earth is delayed or unavailable, reducing dependence on continuous communication with ground-based support teams and promoting collaborative health awareness in isolated environments.

With further testing, the approach could also support health monitoring in remote settings on Earth, such as scientific expeditions, isolated research stations, and communities with limited connectivity.

  1. What tools, languages, hardware, and software did you use?

We built the wearable prototype with an ESP32 microcontroller, electronic components, and sensors for different physiological measurements, integrating embedded systems, software engineering, and experimental biomedical sensing.

The ECG setup uses adhesive electrodes placed on the chest to pick up the heart’s electrical signal. These signals are represented as digital ADC samples without clinical calibration. The prototype also incorporates experimental monitoring of heart rate, estimated oxygen saturation (SpO₂), respiratory rate, and relative body movement, subject to sensor availability and performance.

We used C++ to program the ESP32 firmware, Python and FastAPI for the backend, HTML for the web dashboard, and SQLite to store data locally so the backend can retrieve it without a cloud connection.

We are developing encryption for data transmitted from the ESP32 to FastAPI. Our security design also includes multifactor authentication (MFA) for dashboard access.

Artificial intelligence tools were also used to support the project’s development process, complementing the team’s technical knowledge, problem-solving, and engineering decisions. AI served as a development support tool rather than a clinical diagnostic component.

The architecture is intended to support future expansion, including additional sensors and more advanced data analysis capabilities.

  1. How is your project creative?

A typical smartwatch focuses on one wearer. AstroVital AI uses wearable sensing to give an entire crew one place to review health trends and monitor alerts.

Our innovation lies in transforming individual wearable monitoring into a collaborative crew health ecosystem that combines physiological sensing, contextual information, historical data, and offline operation.

It also puts measurements alongside the astronaut’s own observations. For example, the crew could review an elevated heart rate alongside a check-in about recent physical exertion. That context matters because astronauts perform very different tasks inside a spacecraft, during a spacewalk, and on the lunar surface.

Rather than focusing exclusively on isolated measurements, AstroVital AI emphasizes the relationship between physiological changes, physical activity, perceived well-being, and their evolution over time. This approach is particularly relevant in environments where immediate external medical assistance may not be available.

The project brings together hardware, software, and human-centered design to address the challenges of monitoring crew health beyond Earth, while considering the technological and operational constraints of space exploration.

  1. What factors did your team consider?

We considered intermittent connectivity, variation in physical activity across mission scenarios, the quality of experimental sensor readings, and the privacy of crew health data.
We also used NASA’s five human spaceflight hazards as a conceptual framework to better understand the challenges associated with long-duration missions and contextualize the development of our proposal.

We also considered what an alert needs to communicate quickly: whose reading changed, which signal triggered the alert, and whether the system flagged the measurement as unreliable.

Additional considerations included system scalability, data availability, local storage, information security, and the importance of distinguishing missing or unreliable measurements from valid physiological changes.

Sensor performance and alert thresholds would require clinical validation and mission-specific testing before AstroVital AI could be used operationally or to guide medical decisions.

At its current stage, AstroVital AI is a research and technology demonstration prototype, not a diagnostic medical device or a replacement for professional medical assessment. Its purpose is to explore how integrated technologies can support crew health awareness, collaborative monitoring, and greater autonomy during future space missions.
